Walkthrough: the building blocks

Source: vignettes/articles/walkthrough.Rmd
walkthrough.Rmd

The quickstart runs rcomplex() in one call. This article runs the same analysis step by step on eight Pooideae grasses. Use it when you need to change one step, to inspect an intermediate object, or to run the module and trait tests.

Species Code Life cycle Genus pair
Brachypodium distachyon BDIS annual Brachypodium
Brachypodium sylvaticum BSYL perennial Brachypodium
Hordeum vulgare HVUL annual Hordeum
Hordeum jubatum HJUB perennial Hordeum
Briza maxima BMAX annual Briza
Briza media (mapped to BMAX) BMED perennial Briza
Vulpia bromoides VBRO annual Festuca/Vulpia
Festuca pratensis FPRA perennial Festuca/Vulpia

The data are VST-normalised RNA-seq for the 1,500 most expressed hogs from the “Live or let die?” project, stored as SummarizedExperiment objects. Each species has 20 leaf and 20 root samples.

1. Inputs

We keep the 20 leaf samples. A network built from pooled leaf and root samples mostly separates tissues, so use one tissue per network or remove the tissue with block (see the methods article).

library(rcomplex)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

se_list <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "pooideae_vignette.rds",
  package = "rcomplex"
))
se_list <- lapply(se_list, function(s) s[, s$tissue == "leaf"])
species <- names(se_list)

clades <- list(
  annual = c("BDIS", "HVUL", "BMAX", "VBRO"),
  perennial = c("BSYL", "HJUB", "BMED", "FPRA")
)

clades is a named list of species vectors. Every function that takes a trait or a lineage takes this one shape. clades_from_tree() builds it from a species tree.

The ortholog table has one row per gene: species, gene and hog. Here it comes from rowData(). For an OrthoFinder or PLAZA file, call read_orthologs().

long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(species, function(s) {
  data.frame(
    species = s, gene = rownames(se_list[[s]]),
    hog = as.character(rowData(se_list[[s]])$hog)
  )
}))
long <- long[!is.na(long$hog), ]
tab(head(long, 4))
species gene hog
BDIS Bradi0012s00100.v3.2 HOG:0033476
BDIS Bradi1g00480.v3.2 HOG:0031154
BDIS Bradi1g00552.v3.2 HOG:0027601
BDIS Bradi1g00560.v3.2 HOG:0022846

Paralog reduction

Recent duplicates often have near-identical expression. They inflate the number of cliques without adding information. reduce_orthogroups() merges the paralogs of a hog that correlate above cor_threshold and keeps divergent copies apart.

reduced <- lapply(species, function(s) {
  reduce_orthogroups(
    assay(se_list[[s]], 1), long[long$species == s, c("gene", "hog")],
    gene_col = "gene", cor_threshold = 0.7
  )
})
names(reduced) <- species
vapply(reduced, function(r) r$n_merged, integer(1))
#> BDIS BSYL HVUL HJUB BMAX BMED VBRO FPRA 
#>   95   97  121 1235  131  108  104  126

prepare_orthologs() turns the long table into ortholog pairs and maps the genes through the reduction.

orthologs <- prepare_orthologs(long, reduced)
nrow(orthologs)
#> [1] 93823

2. Networks

compute_network() correlates all gene pairs and converts the correlations to mutual rank (MR). MR asks whether two genes rank each other among their best partners, so a gene that correlates with everything does not dominate. The network keeps the top 3% of gene pairs as edges.

The sparse store holds more pairs than the analysis threshold: store_density = 0.06 leaves room for the density sweep in section 4.

networks <- lapply(reduced, function(r) {
  compute_network(r$expr_matrix, density = 0.03, store_density = 0.06)
})

Each network records the correlation it needed to pass the threshold. At 20 samples this value is low, and many edges are chance correlations.

vapply(networks, function(n) n$params$r_threshold, numeric(1))
#>      BDIS      BSYL      HVUL      HJUB      BMAX      BMED      VBRO      FPRA 
#> 0.3506675 0.3186672 0.2894165 0.3056724 0.3620338 0.3456037 0.3967495 0.2942797

Networks built elsewhere enter through as_network(). Pass a gene by gene matrix of edge weights or a sparse matrix.

3. Co-expressologs

find_coexpressologs() tests every ortholog pair in every species pair. It maps the neighbours of gene A in species 1 to species 2 and asks how many are neighbours of the ortholog of A. The test runs in both directions, and both must pass.

edges <- find_coexpressologs(networks, orthologs, seed = 1)
table(edges$type)
#> 
#> conserved        ns 
#>     23765     69083
tab(head(edges[order(-edges$effect_size), c(
  "gene1", "gene2", "hog", "score", "evalue", "q_value", "effect_size",
  "power"
)], 4))
gene1 gene2 hog score evalue q_value effect_size power
Bradi2g56070.v3.2 HORVU.MOREX.r3.3HG0299740.V3 HOG:0022963 10.621 1.763 0.003 16.258 0.168
Brasyl.3G236800.v2.1 gene-Fpra_egapxtmp_024636 HOG:0011023 9.979 3.217 0.005 15.458 0.136
Brasyl.8G086300.v2.1 HORVU.MOREX.r3.5HG0494330.V3 HOG:0000079 38.715 0.000 0.000 14.957 0.406
VULPIA.BROMOIDES.r1.ctg234G00302340 gene-Fpra_egapxtmp_020959 HOG:0011881 62.910 0.000 0.000 14.944 0.687
  • score is -log2(p) and evalue is n_tests * p.
  • effect_size is the fold enrichment of shared neighbours.
  • power is the chance to call the pair had it been conserved. A non-significant pair with low power is weak evidence of divergence.

type == "conserved" marks a co-expressolog.

Hypergeometric or rank

The default test is the hypergeometric test of ComPlEx. It is fast and matches the published method. method = "rank" ranks every gene in species 2 by its co-expression with the translated neighbours, and reports the ortholog’s place in that ranking. The rank test needs the argument null_networks: one network per species, built by null_network() from the expression with the samples shuffled.

Nulls

coexpressolog_null() rewires each network with the degrees held fixed and repeats the test. It answers how many calls to expect from the degree sequence alone.

nul <- coexpressolog_null(networks, orthologs, n_cores = 2, seed = 1)

rcomplex(null = TRUE) shuffles hog labels among genes of the same expression level and reports calls_null per species pair.

4. Density sweep

A 3% density is a convention. A conserved pair should survive a range of densities. density_sweep() repeats the test at a set of multipliers of the threshold. A multiplier above 1 tightens the network and a multiplier below 1 loosens it. The loosest multiplier must stay inside the stored edges.

multipliers <- seq(0.975, 1.025, by = 0.0125)
store_floor <- max(vapply(
  networks, function(n) n$store_threshold / n$threshold, numeric(1)
))
stopifnot(min(multipliers) >= store_floor)

sweep <- density_sweep(networks, orthologs,
  multipliers = multipliers, method = "hypergeometric", seed = 1
)
tab(sweep[, c("multiplier", "eff_density", "n_significant")])
multiplier eff_density n_significant
0.975 0.052 31923
0.987 0.041 28097
1.000 0.030 23751
1.012 0.020 17918
1.025 0.010 9190

Raw MR values are compressed near the top. A small multiplier moves the effective density a lot. Count, for each hog, how many levels keep a conserved edge:

survive <- table(unlist(lapply(sweep$edges, function(e) {
  unique(e$hog[e$type == "conserved"])
})))
table(factor(survive, levels = seq_len(nrow(sweep))))
#> 
#>    1    2    3    4    5 
#>    3    7   50  278 1162

5. Modules

A module is a group of genes that are co-expressed with each other. detect_modules() runs Leiden clustering. Check that your modules replicate before you test them. At 20 samples they often do not.

modules <- lapply(networks, detect_modules, seed = 42)
vapply(modules, function(m) m$n_modules, integer(1))
#> BDIS BSYL HVUL HJUB BMAX BMED VBRO FPRA 
#>    7    8    9    6    7    7    7    7

as_modules() builds the same object from any gene partition, such as the output of another tool.

Preservation

preservation_paired() asks, for each ordered species pair, whether the modules of the reference species keep their wiring in the partner network. It tests two statistics against a gene-identity permutation null: the density of the module (avg.weight) and the correlation of intramodular connectivity (cor.degree). A module is preserved only when both are significant. Each module is conserved, moderate, diverged or untested.

The trait test in the next section needs all pairs. Pairs between genera supply the same-trait contrasts. n_perm = 500 keeps the example short. Use the default of 10,000 for results you report.

pairs <- as.data.frame(t(utils::combn(species, 2)))
names(pairs) <- c("species1", "species2")

trait <- stack(clades)
trait <- setNames(as.character(trait$ind), trait$values)

pres <- preservation_paired(modules, networks, orthologs,
  pairs = pairs, group = trait, edges = edges, n_perm = 500, seed = 42
)
table(pres$classification$classification)
#> 
#> conserved  diverged  moderate 
#>       254        35       110

Is divergence associated with the trait?

preservation_matrix_test() asks one question of the whole matrix: are trait-discordant pairs the less preserved ones? It compares the mean Zsummary_std of concordant pairs (two annuals or two perennials) with that of discordant pairs. It refers the difference to a null that relabels the traits of the species.

block names the genera. It enables a second null that relabels only within a genus, which holds the phylogeny fixed. It also drops the within-genus pairs, where trait and relatedness are confounded.

genus <- list(
  Brachypodium = c("BDIS", "BSYL"), Hordeum = c("HVUL", "HJUB"),
  Briza = c("BMAX", "BMED"), Festuca = c("VBRO", "FPRA")
)
pmt <- suppressWarnings(preservation_matrix_test(
  pres$classification, trait,
  block = genus, seed = 1
))
tab(pmt$class_means)
class n mean_z
concordant 171 17.805
annual vs perennial 171 17.903 
c(
  observed = pmt$observed, p_free = pmt$p_free, p_blocked = pmt$p_blocked,
  floor_free = pmt$free$p_attainable,
  floor_blocked = pmt$blocked$p_attainable
)
#>      observed        p_free     p_blocked    floor_free floor_blocked 
#>   -0.09869348    0.54285714    0.50000000    0.02857143    0.12500000

A positive statistic means discordant pairs are less preserved. On this data the statistic is near zero, so the leaf modules carry no trait signal. The two nulls agree.

The floor of a relabelling p-value comes from the species set. Eight species split 4/4 give choose(8, 4) = 70 labellings, and two of them share the maximum, so the floor is 2/70 = 0.029. Within four genera the floor is 2/16 = 0.125. No amount of sampling lowers either floor. preservation_matrix_test() warns when the floor exceeds 0.05, and the chunk above silences that warning.

P-value resolution

A permutation p-value cannot fall below 1 / (n_perm + 1). Tests whose true p-value is smaller all return the floor and tie. Rank on Zsummary_std and keep p and q for the significance call. pvalue_resolution() reports the ties:

pvalue_resolution(pres$classification$q_value, n_perm = 500)
#> p-value resolution
#>   values          399
#>   distinct        71 (18% of the values)
#>   minimum         0.002 (77 values tied there)
#>   at 1            0
#>   n_perm          500, floor 1/(n_perm + 1) = 0.002
#>   status          permutation-limited: the minimum IS the floor
#>   off grid        259 values are not multiples of the floor
#> 
#>   77 values are tied at 0.002 and carry NO ordering among themselves.
#>   Ranking, weighting or top-k selection over that block reads tie-break
#>   noise, not evidence.
#>   Rank on a continuous effect size instead -- Zsummary_std from
#>   module_preservation() -- and keep the p-value for the significance call
#>   alone.
#>   Separating the tie needs n_perm >= 50000. That is a lower bound: the
#>   true p-values may lie far further below the floor.

6. Hubs

identify_module_hubs() finds the hub genes of each module. The primary centrality is the weighted degree. It also reports betweenness and eigenvector centrality.

hubs <- lapply(species, function(s) {
  identify_module_hubs(modules[[s]], networks[[s]], orthologs)
})
names(hubs) <- species
vapply(hubs, function(h) sum(h$is_hub), integer(1))
#> BDIS BSYL HVUL HJUB BMAX BMED VBRO FPRA 
#>  187  191  184  277  182  184  195  204

classify_hub_conservation() labels each hog by where it is a hub. It needs module_correspondence(), which tests which module of species 1 matches which module of species 2. Reuse the ortholog map that preservation_paired() resolved. The key is the sorted species pair.

pairs_genus <- lapply(genus, sort)
correspondence <- lapply(pairs_genus, function(sp) {
  key <- paste(sp, collapse = ".")
  module_correspondence(modules[[sp[1]]], modules[[sp[2]]],
    pres$raw[[key]]$map,
    species_ref = sp[1], species_test = sp[2], seed = 1
  )
})
names(correspondence) <- vapply(
  pairs_genus, paste, character(1), collapse = "."
)

hub_class <- classify_hub_conservation(hubs, clades,
  module_comparisons = correspondence
)
table(hub_class$classification)
#> 
#>    annual_specific_hub          conserved_hub        multi_trait_hub 
#>                     99                     36                      1 
#>                non_hub perennial_specific_hub            rewired_hub 
#>                    630                    124                      7 
#>           sporadic_hub 
#>                    603

get_coexpressed_hogs() lists the hogs that co-express with a candidate hub in several species.

candidate <- hub_class$hog[hub_class$classification == "conserved_hub"][1]
partners <- get_coexpressed_hogs(candidate, networks, orthologs,
  clades = clades, min_species = 2L, edges = edges
)
tab(head(partners[, c(
  "partner_hog", "n_species", "coexpressed_traits", "partner_min_q"
)], 5))
partner_hog n_species coexpressed_traits partner_min_q
HOG:0016566 8 annual,perennial 0
HOG:0020610 8 annual,perennial 0
HOG:0018221 8 annual,perennial 0
HOG:0017319 8 annual,perennial 0
HOG:0011649 8 annual,perennial 0

7. Cliques

A clique is a set of genes, one per species, that are all co-expressed with each other. The edges of one hog form a graph, and rcomplex finds cliques on it in two ways. The two answer different questions.

Species graph

find_cliques() cliques the graph of species. It returns one best gene assignment per clique. Give it the full edge table, so the intensity scale uses every tested pair.

cliques <- find_cliques(edges, species, min_species = 2L)
table(cliques$n_species)
#> 
#>    2    3    4    5    6    7    8 
#> 2542 1213  523  303  214  127   90

A clique of two species is a single conserved edge. Cliques that span three or more species need conservation across independent lineages.

clique_stability() removes k species at a time and checks whether each clique persists. A clique that survives the removal of any one species does not depend on a single lineage.

stab <- clique_stability(edges, species,
  clades = clades, all_species = species,
  full_cliques = cliques, max_k = 2L
)
table(stab$stability_class)
#> 
#>    0    1    2 
#> 1558  322 3132

classify_cliques() assigns each hog to one class: complete (all species), partial (both clades, not all species), differentiated (a clique in each clade and none across), trait_specific (one clade only) or unclassified. The underpowered column flags a differentiated or trait_specific call that rests on edges with low power.

result <- classify_cliques(edges, species, clades,
  min_species = 2L, stability = stab
)
table(result$classification)
#> 
#>       complete differentiated        partial trait_specific   unclassified 
#>             90              6           1315             41             48

Gene graph

gene_clique_graph() cliques the graph of genes. A hog with paralogs gives one clique per gene combination. It returns three tables: cliques has one row per clique, members one row per clique member, and twins one row per collapsed twin. Twins are paralogs with the same partners; one clique stands for all their combinations (multiplicity). classify_gene_cliques() applies the six-tier taxonomy of Rodriguez et al. (2026): complete_conserved, lineage_specific, partial_significant, partial_present, differentiated and trait_specific. A clique that fits none is unclassified. A tier that rests on low power becomes underpowered.

gene_cliques <- gene_clique_graph(edges)
#> gene_clique_graph: 3 ortholog groups exceeded 10 genes in some species; 16 genes dropped
#> gene_clique_graph: 145 genes collapsed into 71 twin classes; cliques carry multiplicity
gene_class <- classify_gene_cliques(gene_cliques, edges, species,
  clades = clades
)
table(gene_class$classification)
#> 
#> complete_conserved    partial_present     trait_specific       unclassified 
#>                265                 32                 16               6790 
#>       underpowered 
#>                 13

Pass the unfiltered edge table. The gap tiers need the pairs that were tested and failed, so they can refuse them.

Use the species graph for stability and for one clique per hog. Use the gene graph to see every paralog combination and to follow the published taxonomy. The species graph finds more trait_specific hogs because it asks for a clique among the species it can see, and the gene graph asks for a complete clique of one clade with an outside species tested at adequate power.

8. Reading the results

Combine the robustness signals. A hog with a complete class, a stability class of 2 or more, and survival at most density levels is a strong candidate.

result$n_densities <- as.integer(survive[result$hog])
result$n_densities[is.na(result$n_densities)] <- 0L
keep <- result$classification == "complete" &
  result$stability_class >= 2L &
  result$n_densities >= nrow(sweep) - 1L
strong <- result[keep, ]
nrow(strong)
#> [1] 87
tab(head(strong[order(strong$best_mean_q), c(
  "hog", "n_species", "best_mean_q", "stability_class", "n_densities"
)], 5))
hog n_species best_mean_q stability_class n_densities
HOG:0028978 8 0 2 5
HOG:0020610 8 0 2 5
HOG:0018534 8 0 2 5
HOG:0011862 8 0 2 5
HOG:0021123 8 0 2 5

Check three things before you believe any result.

  1. Read the correlation each network needed (r_threshold).
  2. Read the power of the edges behind a negative call.
  3. Read pvalue_resolution() for every permutation p-value.

The methods article gives the statistics behind each step.
